newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin vows to bypass Duma opposition to reform.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin vows to bypass Duma opposition to reform.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday he would ignore opposition in parliament to his market reforms and press ahead with them regardless.

"Regretfully, the deputies have not supported the decision which is needed and have been afraid to shoulder responsibility for these painful but vitally important measures," Yeltsin said in a radio address.
"We will do all that is necessary with regard to this decision."

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament went on summer holiday earlier this week after rejecting most of the government-proposed draft laws aimed at boosting market reforms and putting state finances in order.
Yeltsin, whose address focused on the elderly, said the bills were aimed at securing enough money in the budget to prevent a recurrence of the problem of pensions being delayed for months.

His remarks suggested he was ready to use his vast constitutional powers to push through at least some of the changes by decree. Yeltsin could issue decrees on specific reform packages but not on the entire budget.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Thursday the government had fulfilled Yeltsin's demand to pay off arrears on old age pensions by July 1. Chubais has also threatened to bypass the Duma.
Ministers have blamed poor tax collection for the pension and wage arrears that have helped fuel social discontent across the vast Russian Federation.

Chubais, who is also finance minister, said the last money transfer of 2.75 trillion roubles ($477.3 million) in pension arrears was made on Wednesday. He did not say how much money the pensioners had been owed.
He added that Russia's Savings Bank and commercial banks would be working all weekend to deliver the money to pensioners.

Yeltsin, who last week dedicated his radio address to the problems of the young, said Russia needed youthful and energetic people but should not overlook the needs of the elderly in the headlong rush towards a market economy.
"Reforms have been most painful for people of the older generation," Yeltsin said. "I have to accept some of the blame for this."
Yeltsin said it was clear the government was not able to pay adequate pensions in the long term and reform would be needed.
"But there will not be any sudden changes," he said. "Pension reform will take place smoothly and slowly and will take several decades."
